src.t.ditffc: Open the 📋 board. Code tasks are on the laptop, the bench stand and the ground station are on the rack.
src.t.1io8rkt: Four, so it can steer by speeding some up and slowing others down. Tip it right: speed up the left pair. Nose down: speed up the rear pair.
src.t.shmu3x: And two spin clockwise, two counter-clockwise, because a spinning prop twists the body the other way, like me stirring a tea and the glass wanting to turn. The twists cancel; speed one pair up to turn on purpose.
src.t.1ita9vs: The mixer is just who does what for each command. One sign wrong and the drone does the opposite of what it is told, which at five hundred times a second is over very quickly.
src.t.geg6xn: Two witnesses. The gyro says how fast you turn; add that up and you have the angle. Smooth, but it has a tiny constant error, so after a minute it is sure you are upside down.
src.t.m34d50: The accelerometer feels where gravity pulls. Right on average, but jumpy, and when the drone itself speeds up it cannot tell a push from a tilt. Like tea slopping in a glass when the bus brakes: it thinks the table is tilted.
src.t.1eiic1a: So: trust the gyro for the quick part, the accelerometer for the slow part. A complementary filter does that with one number. A Kalman filter does it with maths, and also learns the gyro’s error.
src.t.qrfcsj: Because the motors hum at about a hundred and twenty-five times a second and shake the chip. Gossip with a lawnmower going in the background.
src.t.fa59ty: A notch filter removes only that one hum and costs almost nothing. A low-pass smooths everything but makes the signal late, and late is dangerous in a loop that corrects five hundred times a second.
src.t.9keg0o: If the hum gets through, the D term amplifies it and the motors jitter and get hot. You can measure that in degrees on the motor.
src.t.2u5wrg: P pushes in proportion to the error: the further off, the harder. I remembers errors that stay, D reacts to how fast the error is changing and calms things down.
src.t.d048fq: Two loops: the outer one says how fast to turn to reach the angle, the inner one pushes the motors to turn at exactly that speed. Like telling someone “head for the door” and then them adjusting each step.
src.t.1xv1svh: Turn the gains up and it reacts faster, until the delays catch up: the motor lag, the speed controller’s update rate. Then it overshoots, corrects too much, and rings.
src.t.1utke7j: And on the pad: the integrator adds up the error while the drone sits tilted and cannot move. At take-off it empties it all at once. That is windup.
src.t.1jsvfg2: The camera sits on two little servos that turn against the drone, like carrying a tray while the floor rocks.
src.t.9n01nh: Feedback alone only reacts after the camera has already moved. Feed-forward knows the drone’s tilt and moves the servos at the same time. Both together is best: the first does the work and the second tidies up.
src.t.16iowhi: It is a thin pipe, about three and a half thousand bytes a second. Telemetry goes down it, and so do the heartbeats that tell the drone the ground station is alive.
src.t.50ndqk: Ask for fifty updates a second and the pipe is full. Packets drop, heartbeats too, and after a few seconds the drone decides the link is dead and flies home, in the middle of the delivery. Ten a second is plenty to watch.
src.t.lx2jsl: It decides by itself. No heartbeat for a few seconds: fly the route back and land at home. Battery low: go home while there is still some left to get there. Reach the fence round the boss’s office: turn around.
src.t.1cg6lsh: Wait too long to give up and the battery is gone before it is home. Wait too short and a lost packet sends it home for nothing. Hovering sounds safe, until the battery runs out and it lands in the ceiling fan.
src.t.18heilm: Sensors in, motors out, five hundred times a second. The ground station watches and has the failsafes. Don’t let it near the office.
src.t.1eu95r3: The IMU is a tiny chip with a gyro and an accelerometer. The gyro says how fast you turn, the accelerometer says which way gravity pulls. Like a waiter with a very good inner ear.
src.t.1jll532: Both are shaken by the motors’ hum, so we filter them first, but every filter makes the signal a little late.
src.t.1ivyddy: Two liars, one angle. The gyro is smooth but wanders off; the accelerometer is right on average but jumpy, and fooled whenever the drone itself accelerates.
src.t.nog4ze: The estimator takes the gyro for the quick part and the accelerometer for the slow part. Get the mix wrong and it believes it is level while it is not.
src.t.yp5a1d: The outer loop asks: how far am I from where I want to lean? It answers with how fast to turn.
src.t.7163ty: Too gentle and the drone is lazy; too keen and it overshoots like a waiter with a full tray.
src.t.1dvu0b4: The inner loop is fast and does the actual work: it compares how fast we are turning with how fast we were asked to, and pushes the motors to close the gap.
src.t.55kt7x: D damps the ringing but also amplifies the hum, which heats the motors.
src.t.1lf7q3j: Three commands and a throttle become four motor speeds. To roll right, the left motors speed up and the right ones slow down.
src.t.mdtj32: Two props spin each way so their twisting pushes cancel. Yaw is just speeding up one pair and slowing the other.
src.t.n8l00w: Each motor has an ESC, a speed controller. How often it hears a new command matters: old PWM listens fifty times a second, DShot thousands.
src.t.178nbr0: And a motor takes a moment to speed up. All that delay is why the gains cannot be turned all the way up.
src.t.1l6r5ww: The camera sits on two little servos that turn against the drone’s tilt, like carrying a glass of tea while the floor rocks.
src.t.16xxr5t: It does best when it knows what the drone is about to do (feed-forward) and also checks what the camera really sees (feedback).
src.t.10ry6pr: The ground station is the laptop screen you fly it from: the map, the buttons, the mission. It refuses to arm a drone nobody has calibrated on the bench.
src.t.53pdel: A thin radio carries telemetry down and heartbeats up. Ask for too much telemetry and it clogs, the heartbeats go missing and the drone thinks the link is dead.
src.t.mx8amp: When no one is at the controls, the drone decides for itself. No heartbeat for a few seconds: go home. Battery low: go home while there is still some. Reach the fence round the boss’s office: turn around.
src.t.1w2u08r: Demo time. Show me Çay-Kopter. And it better not crash.
src.t.120h92g: It has been going round and round for an hour and plays a song. A *sad* song. Who taught it sad?
src.t.1u36mg7: The poor thing. It thinks it is in the kitchen. Tea will not fix it, but tea will not hurt.
src.t.dcwhew: Listen up. Photos. Everyone edits photos. *We* send them to a man called Selim who edits them for forty lira. That ends today.
src.t.td778z: It’s called *Fotoşop*. Like the famous one, but I’ve already written the pricing: seven lira a month, per layer, and the undo is a premium feature. Legal says that’s “brave”.
src.t.1r2t5pp: Layers, filters, a slider that shows before and after. The slider is the whole demo. Also: my face on every photo. With the scratch removed. I have a scratch.
src.t.1xidcsu: Tea, anyone? Tip: a photo is not “what it looks like”. It’s numbers, and the numbers need a note saying what they mean. Keep your eye on the *edges*: of layers, of the picture, of the cache.
src.t.ikyx1c: I’ll take the maths of blending. Someone want the blur? It’s the filter everybody’s filter is made of.
src.t.1boaiux: Because the numbers in a photo are not amounts of light. They are squeezed: a file stores 0.5 for a tone that is only a fifth as bright as 1.0, because your eye notices differences in the dark far more than in the bright.
src.t.3n4nf5: Half a lamp on is 0.735 in the file. If you average the *numbers* you get 0.5, which is a quarter of the light. Dark fringes on soft edges, muddy gradients: that is why. Decode to light, blend, encode again.
src.t.a16pc4: *Multiply* is two glasses of tea stacked: the light has to pass through both, so it only ever gets darker. *Screen* is two lamps pointed at one wall: it only ever gets lighter. *Overlay* does multiply to the dark half and screen to the bright half, so contrast goes up.
src.t.grhxgy: Same formulas whatever the space. What changes the look is whether you run them on light or on the stored numbers.
src.t.ef67s4: A blur is each pixel becoming the weighted average of the pixels around it. Done square-style, a radius of 8 means 17 times 17: 289 sums for every pixel.
src.t.1kevyjq: A Gaussian has a trick: blur along the rows, then along the columns, and you get the exact same picture with 17 plus 17 sums. Like serving a whole floor: first every row, then every column, instead of every person against every other.
src.t.92d47t: A pixel that is not there still has a colour in the file: black. Blur the colours alone and that black seeps into the edge.
src.t.63920u: The fix is *premultiplied alpha*: multiply the colour by its opacity first, so see-through counts for nothing, blur, and divide it back out. Like diluting tea with water: you must count how much tea is in the glass, not just how brown it is.
src.t.3ym60p: It has to look at neighbours that do not exist. You must make them up. *Clamp* repeats the last pixel. *Mirror* reflects the picture. *Wrap* takes the opposite side. *Zero* says everything out there is black.
src.t.ewy0s8: Zero gives the picture a dark frame after a blur. Wrap leaks the left edge into the right. Clamp is the quiet one: the last pixel is the best guess for the next.
src.t.1jfdlx8: Blur the photo, subtract the blur from the original, and what is left is the detail. Add some of the detail back. The name is from darkrooms: they used a blurry negative as a mask.
src.t.rrlhhf: Radius is how fat the detail is, amount how much you add, threshold lets you skip tiny differences like grain. Too much amount and the pixels run out of range, burnt to pure black or white, with halos beside every edge.
src.t.umhlaz: Count how many pixels are at each brightness and draw it as bars. A hazy photo is a hill pushed into one corner: the darkest pixel is not black and the brightest not white.
src.t.1qs6jvd: Levels pull the black point and the white point to where the hill starts and ends. Every tone gets stretched to fill the range. Pull too far and the ends are cut off: those pixels are clipped, and detail there is gone for good.
src.t.l16fsl: A file says “0.9, 0.3, 0.1”. Which red? sRGB is the plain screen’s idea. Display P3 is the phone screen’s richer idea. The same numbers mean different colours.
src.t.1tjm3fd: Read a P3 file as sRGB and everything is dull. Read an sRGB file as P3 and it is garish. The profile in the file is the note that tells you which: read it, then convert to what the screen shows.
src.t.1fbzrb8: It does not invent. It looks around the hole, finds a place in the photo whose neighbours look just like the hole’s neighbours, and copies what is there. On a brick wall that finds another brick and mortar joint.
src.t.ao5g46: The lazy version fills one average colour: the scratch is gone and a plaster is left. Ask me how I know.
src.t.1ub0rk4: A 24-megapixel photo is 96 megabytes. Fifty undo steps would be nearly five gigabytes. The machine would sit down and cry.
src.t.11bsuy6: But a brush stroke only changes a few squares of the picture. Cut the photo into tiles, and for each step save only the tiles it touched: about a megabyte. The tiles also let you draw only what is on the screen, and keep the last ones warm in a cache.
src.t.i08n06: JPEG cuts the picture into 8-by-8 squares and writes each as a mix of waves, from broad to fine. Then it rounds the numbers, the fine waves harder, because your eye misses them.
src.t.1394gdl: Quality is how hard it rounds. At about 85 you save most of the size and nobody sees. At 30 you see the squares. At 100 you keep everything, including grain, and the file is huge. PNG keeps all of it, exactly.
src.t.zk94gr: A photo comes in, goes through tone, healing and filters, sits in layers, and goes out. Nine boxes. The rest is pixels.
src.t.1v9vcgm: A photo is a grid of numbers plus a note saying what the numbers mean: the colour profile. Lose the note and the colours drift.
src.t.ex4h7i: Levels stretch a hazy photo so it uses the whole range from black to white. The profile says how to turn the file’s numbers into the screen’s colours.
src.t.vuet9r: The healing brush looks around for a piece of the photo whose surroundings match the hole’s, and copies it in. Bricks stay bricks.
src.t.1kencyl: Filters average each pixel with its neighbours. A Gaussian can be done as a row pass and a column pass, which is much faster. At the photo’s border you must decide what lies beyond.
src.t.12efbgv: Layers are sheets of glass with a picture and an alpha. Each pixel is mixed with what is below it by the blend mode. Do the mixing in light, and a half-lit lamp is half as bright to the eye.
src.t.d9bnt5: A 24-megapixel photo is far too big to redraw as one piece. It is cut into tiles, and only the ones on the screen are decoded; recently used ones stay in a cache.
src.t.qf26q0: Undo has to remember what each step changed. Keeping a whole copy per step is 96 megabytes each; keeping only the tiles the brush touched is about one.
src.t.4zta4a: What you see: the layers blended and converted to the screen’s colours.
src.t.5bs6p0: Export squeezes the picture into a file. JPEG throws away detail the eye misses, in 8-by-8 blocks, and quality says how much to throw away. Too much and the blocks show.
src.t.1t1si3o: Demo time. Show me Fotoşop. And it better not crash.
src.t.1qewpfq: It must play without stuttering, my lips must match my voice, and the file must fit in an email. I do not know what a keyframe is and I will not be told.
src.t.vhv2x6: Tea, anyone? Tip: video is a stack of lies told 30 times a second. Frames lean on frames, sound is cut into pieces that do not divide, and light is not what the numbers say. Check each one.
src.t.wlcbr9: I already cut the first minute. With scissors. On a printout.
src.t.uihbfb: Because the camera lies about its speed. It makes 29.97 frames a second, but a timecode wants a round 30 to a “second”. After an hour the label is 108 frames ahead of the wall clock, which is three and a half seconds of a boss saying “synergy”.
src.t.2jiymw: Drop-frame fixes the label, not the picture: two numbers (:00 and :01) are skipped at the start of every minute, except every tenth. Like a bus that skips two stops to keep to the timetable. No frame is thrown away, only the names.
src.t.mvc11w: A picture lasts 1601.6 samples of sound. You cannot hand out six tenths of a sample, so you round. Round down every time and you lose six tenths a frame. A half-hour interview is fifty-four thousand frames: that is most of a second.
src.t.xae9e5: The cure is to keep the change: 1602, 1601, 1602, 1601, 1602, which makes 8008 over five frames, exactly. Like paying a bill with coins: you never round each coffee, you settle at the end of the day.
src.t.2p0p56: A LUT is a look-up table: the colourist did the grading once, and wrote it down as “if you see this, show that”. She did it watching a screen, so the table speaks screen numbers.
src.t.1yb5mzo: Our pixels are in light, a different scale: double the number, double the light. Feed light into a table written for screens and the dark tones, which take up very little room in light, all fall into the first row of the table. Black soup. Encode first, then look up.
src.t.ezmpjg: For each pixel: how much greener is it than its red and blue? A lot, it is screen. Not at all, it is boss. In between, it is a hair or an edge, so you fade it out instead of cutting, a *soft* key.
src.t.yxh5n1: Two traps. Start the key too late and the dark corners of the sheet stay; too early and his dark suit starts to vanish. And the green light bounces off the sheet onto him: *spill*. Despill pulls the green down on whatever stays. Like wiping my tea off the saucer before I serve it.
src.t.v06ec1: Screen numbers are squeezed: half of the number is not half of the light. If you fade by averaging the numbers, the middle is darker than the real average of the two lights. A brown slush between a red and a green.
src.t.1nndlb2: Turn them back into light, mix, and squeeze again. And ease the curve: if it moves at one speed from the first frame to the last, the eye feels the start and the end like a lift pulling off. Smooth: slow, quick, slow.
src.t.1ra0l4v: A camera file saves space by telling you only what changed. Every few seconds there is a whole picture, the keyframe. The frames after it say “same as before, but the cup moved”. To show one frame you start at the last whole picture and replay everything since.
src.t.1kanzzy: Going forward you carry on from where you were. Going back, you start again from the keyframe, every step. The fix is a proxy: a smaller copy where *every* frame is a whole picture. Bigger on disk, instant to jump about in. And a cache remembers what you just showed, as long as it fits in memory.
src.t.famw0j: The encoder cuts the picture in little squares and writes each as a sum of patterns, from broad to fine. The fine ones the eye hardly sees, so they are rounded to zero, and zeros cost nothing to store. The bigger the rounding step, the smaller the file and the worse the picture.
src.t.rj4par: PSNR measures how far the result is from the original, in decibels. Forty is clean, thirty is soft. Constant bitrate gives every frame the same bits, even when a dissolve needs more. Variable spends them where the picture is hard. And a keyframe is expensive, so too many wastes bits, and too few makes seeking slow.
src.t.14x4hxl: Footage in, picture and sound lined up, effects, a viewer, an encoder. Eight boxes. Look at the timeline. Don’t look at the audio. I have a call.
src.t.1yt9g9b: The footage as it came off the camera: tea being poured, the boss’s keynote on a green screen, and a cat. Big files, squeezed over long stretches.
src.t.imef3h: Editing on the originals is like asking a busy man to retell his story from the beginning each time. Proxies are cheap copies made for editing, and a cache remembers what was just shown.
src.t.164mgo2: The timeline places each shot by timecode. A timecode counts 30 frames a second, the camera makes 29.97: the label has to skip two numbers a minute to stay true.
src.t.ry5g6r: Sound is cut into pieces to sit under each picture. A picture lasts 1601.6 samples, so some get 1602 and some 1601; do it evenly or the voice drifts away from the lips.
src.t.a3swir: Takes the green out of the boss: the more a pixel is greener than its red and blue, the more it is screen. Soft edges keep his hair, despill takes the green off his suit.
src.t.1xysgfu: The colourist’s look arrives as a table. It was made on pictures as seen on a screen, so linear pixels must be encoded first, or the blacks are crushed.
src.t.4iao0p: Where two shots meet, the first melts into the second. Mixed in light it stays bright; eased, it starts and stops without a jolt.
src.t.1yo70f: The viewer plays the edit. At 30 frames a second it has 33 milliseconds per frame, and a dissolve doubles the work.
src.t.znkfgo: Squeezes the picture to fit the premiere site’s 30 MB. It keeps the numbers that matter and zeroes the rest; PSNR tells how much was lost.
src.t.k09udp: The premiere. One boss, one beach, and a link that must open on a phone.
src.t.cjm0dv: Demo time. Show me Premier Çay. And it better not crash.
src.t.fcq3jc: Premier Çay. Cut, grade and export the keynote. Premiere night is Friday; the boss wants a beach.
src.t.1lzb9y0: I am on a beach. My suit is green only slightly. Rıza says that is “spill”. I say that is “brand colour”.
src.t.r9ku0p: Not one dropped frame, and the dissolve is bright all the way. I felt something.
src.t.zggdzh: Frames lean on frames, sound does not divide, and light is not what the numbers say. Look at the tips.
src.t.prtj0r: My lips say “synergy” and the voice says it a second later. Like a bad dub of my own life.
src.t.1pngmd2: Listen up. Drones. Everyone has one. *We* have a glass of tea and a garage. That changes by Friday.
src.t.1yb9mzn: It’s called *Çay-Kopter*. It picks up my tea, flies it across the garage to the table, and films the whole thing in 4K. For the shareholders.
src.t.kx4szu: I read that drones have a “flight controller”. Fine. I want a flight *manager*. And no hitting my office. I just had it painted.
src.t.1y576cu: Four propellers, a tiny chip that feels which way is down, and software that fixes its balance five hundred times a second. Get one sign wrong in the mixer and it flips before it leaves the pad.
src.t.8irs87: I’ll take the ground station. Radios are just very slow WiFi, right?
src.t.1qxf6y5: I can do the codec bits. Someone take the timecode?
